newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli shares down sharply in early trading.
newsitem.headline: Israeli shares down sharply in early trading.

text.p: Israeli shares were down sharply in early trading on Tuesday as the market worried about the imminent appointment of Ariel Sharon as finance minister and concerns about interest rates, traders said.
The benchmark Mishtanim index of top 100 shares was off 1.84 percent on moderate turnover, while the Maof 25 blue chip index was down 1.53 percent.
"Sharon worries the market a lot," said Gad Hacker of Betucha Securities. "He's big spender who spends on ideology and doesn't believe in austere budgets or in liberal economic policy."
The former general is widely expected to get the finance portfolio in the next few days after the resignation of Dan Meridor last week.

Hacker also cited the weakness of Israeli shares traded in New York on Monday. Among the biggest losers in early trading were Koor Industries, down 2.25 percent, and Clal Electronic Industries, down 3.0 percent.
Eyal Kolka of Sigma Securities said the market was concerned that the depreciation of the shekel that began at the end of last week was getting out of hand.
He said that if the currency continued to weaken and Sharon posed a threat to fiscal discipline, the Bank of Israel would hold or even raise interest rates.
The central bank cut the base rate 1.2 percentage points to 12.7 percent in a surprise move last Wednesday.
In the domestic forex market on Tuesday, the dollar was trading at about 3.5402 to the dollar in the early afternoon, up from 3.4979 at the close on Tuesday.
The depreciation was nevertheless giving export-oriented stocks a boost, said Kokla. Makhteshim Chemicals Works and Tadiran Ltd were both up 0.5 percent.
Kokla said he still believed the dominant factor in the market continued to be profit-taking following the market's run-up and that the direction would change.
"There is a consensus in the market that the basic trend is still positive," he said.

"There's uncertainty. The market is nervous that perhaps the best is behind us," said Hacker, adding that he expected the atmosphere to remain nervous over the next several days. Nevertheless, he said the long-term outlook was still good.
- David Rosenberg, Tel Aviv newsroom, 972-3-537-2211 x233
